fields.meta_title: Therapy Intake Form Builder for Counselors | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a therapy intake form that scores screeners, keeps each partner's answers private and matches new clients to a clinician. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Therapy Intake Form Your Clinicians Can Act On
fields.hero_description: Create a therapy intake form that totals the PHQ-9, alerts a clinician to urgent answers, and saves responses to your database.
fields.features_heading: What the Online Form Adds to a Therapy Packet
fields.features_subheading: Six parts of the form that change what a clinician knows before the client sits down.
fields.feature_1:
Screeners scored on submit

Add the PHQ-9 or GAD-7, or any questionnaire your clinicians already score by hand. Each total is added up when the client submits and saved beside the answers it came from.
fields.feature_2:
Separate links for two people

Send each partner, or a teen and a parent, a link of their own. Each person sees only their own questions, and the clinician reads both responses together on one screen.
fields.feature_3:
Consent pages clients sign

Give informed consent and your confidentiality policy a page each after the final question. Clients sign every page with a typed or drawn signature, saved with the date signed.
fields.feature_4:
Matching to a clinician

Compare what the client wants help with, and how they want to meet, against each clinician's specialties, and openings. Clients see who can take them; the rest go to intake.
fields.feature_5:
Alerts on answers that need a person

Alert whoever owns an answer by email or in Slack: the clinical director for a safety question, or the billing lead for an insurance plan outside your practice's network.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take with you

Export the form, its scoring rules, and the database to your GitHub on paid plans. A developer can host it on servers your practice controls or keep editing it outside Emergent.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Counseling Practices Run Intake
fields.tab_content_1:
New clients choose from clinicians who can see them

Larkspur Counseling Group asks each new client what brings them in and whether they want telehealth. Submitting shows the clinicians who treat that concern and have an opening, and the client books one on the same screen. Anyone the rules cannot place goes to Rosa Delgado, the intake coordinator, who calls.
fields.tab_content_2:
Partners never read each other's answers

Harbor Lane Couples Therapy sends each partner a separate link to one intake. Each answers alone, including a rating of the relationship out of 10, and neither can open the other's response. The therapist reads both side by side. Booking for the first joint session opens once both forms are in.
fields.tab_content_3:
The first session waits for a guardian's signature

Fernwood Teen Counseling splits its adolescent intake between teen and parent. The teen answers school and sleep questions on a private link, and only the counselor sees them. The parent adds family history and signs the consent for treatment. Until that signature arrives, nobody can book the first session.
fields.tab_content_4:
Scored screeners, and one answer that cannot wait

Northgate Community Mental Health puts the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 inside its adult intake, and both totals are scored on submit. Any answer other than "Not at all" on PHQ-9 item 9, the question about thoughts of self-harm, alerts Dr. Owen Marsh, the clinical director, to call the client that day.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Therapy Intake Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan a therapy intake form around your screeners and consent pages before you build and test it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List what you ask in session one
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Order pages from easy to hard
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Add the screeners you already score
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Give couples and teens two links
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the questions you ask a new client out loud in the first 20 minutes. Any of them a client can answer alone at home belongs on the form. Keep the ones that need a conversation, like the story behind the presenting concern, for the session.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Start with contact details and an emergency contact, which take a minute. Move on to why the client is seeking therapy and any past treatment. Put heavier history like trauma or substance use near the end, where a client can skip a question and raise it in session.
fields.howto_step_3_des: If your clinicians score the PHQ-9 or the GAD-7 by hand at intake, put them in the form exactly as published, with the same answer choices. Decide where each total should appear and which single answer has to reach a person before the session.
fields.howto_step_4_des: For couples, give each partner a private form. For a client under 18, split the form into a teen part and a parent part. Rules on when a minor can consent to therapy without a parent vary by state. Confirm yours before deciding who signs.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write the prompt the way you would brief a new intake coordinator: which pages come in what order, which screeners to score, who hears about which answer. Emergent builds the form and its response database from that brief. Edit any of it later with another prompt.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Put consent on the last pages
fields.howto_step_6_des: Close with informed consent and the limits of confidentiality, each signed on its own page. The APA Ethics Code asks psychologists to discuss those limits at the outset of the relationship. Have your clinical lead or counsel approve the wording before clients sign.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test it as each kind of client
fields.howto_step_7_des: Submit a test response on a phone for every kind of client you see. Trigger the item 9 alert on purpose. Check that it reaches the right clinician, and that booking stays closed until the consent is signed.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is practice PDFs (an individual adult packet, an adolescent packet, a university clinic, two counseling centers' download pages), a practice-network guide and one AI-intake blog. They all list the same sections and stop at the paper. None deals with what makes therapy intake different from a medical packet: two people on one case (partners, a teen and a parent), screening questionnaires that need scoring, and a client who has to be matched to a clinician. This page names the sections and what each is for, then shows four practices where the online form handles those jobs.
